summary: Addresses how GMPLS and RSVP-TE apply to the overlay model, a user-network interface where clients request paths from a transport network without sharing routing information. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A customer asks a phone company to set up a connection without seeing how the company builds it. This memo explains how to ask.

questions: what is the gmpls overlay model
how does rsvp-te work between edge and core nodes
subtitle: How edge nodes ask a GMPLS core network for connections using RSVP-TE, without seeing inside the core.

tldr.problem: In the overlay model, edge nodes outside a core network must request label switched paths across it, but they do not take part in the core's routing and may not be allowed to see or control everything the core does.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC keeps standard GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling from RFC 3473 and says where the edge-to-core interface differs: shared address space, optional handling of explicit routes and record routes, notification filtering, graceful deletion and VPN-style connections.
tldr.outcome: Core nodes may hide topology and filter RSVP objects from edge nodes, which gives a UNI that can evolve independently of the signaling inside the core. This is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Edge-to-core ERO allowed
facts.value: Ingress edge, ingress core, egress core, egress edge only

today: RFC 4208 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Overlay Model and the UNI
sections.content:
Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) defines routing and signaling protocols for creating Label Switched Paths (LSPs). In a peer model, edge nodes run both routing and signaling, and an edge node talks to a core node the same way two core nodes talk. In the overlay model, the core acts more as a closed system. Edge nodes do not join the core's routing instance and do not know the core topology, although a routing exchange of reachability information to other edge nodes may happen.

This memo covers RSVP-TE procedures between an edge node and its adjacent core node. All signaling is identical to the GMPLS extensions in RFC 3473 except where this document says otherwise. How a link is requested or used by the overlay network is out of scope.

The model can be applied at the User-Network Interface (UNI) of the ASON architecture, where the core is a service provider network and edge nodes are user devices. A single end-to-end RSVP session carries the user parameters, with the first and last hops forming the UNI. That means user parameters need not be mapped into the format of the network-to-network interface, so the UNI and NNI stay independent.
sections.eli5: Customers outside the network can ask it to build a connection, but the inside of the network stays private. Only the first and last steps are shared with the customer.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
An edge node and its attached core node must share the same address space, the one GMPLS uses to signal between edge nodes across the core. This may be the core's own space or a VPN space that the core supports. The core nodes' own address space need not be shared with any edge-node and core-node pair. With several overlay networks on one core, separate address spaces may be used for privacy.

An edge node is identified either by a single IP address as its Node-ID, or by one or more numbered TE links to the core. An edge node needs only its own address, its adjacent core node's address, and the address of any other edge node it wants to reach. A core node needs to track only the addresses on interfaces to its attached edge nodes, their Node IDs, and those of other edge nodes it may connect them to.

The ingress edge node puts either its Node-ID or the address of a numbered TE link in the SENDER_TEMPLATE. In the second case the connection is made only over that interface. The SESSION object likewise carries the egress Node-ID or an egress numbered link address, and its Extended_Tunnel_ID is set to zero or to an address of the ingress edge device.
sections.eli5: The customer and the front desk must use the same kind of address labels. The front desk only needs to know addresses of its own customers and who they are allowed to ship to.

sections.title: Explicit Route Object Handling
sections.content:
An edge node MAY include an Explicit Route Object (ERO) in a Path message, and a core node MAY reject one, depending on configuration. If it rejects because an ERO is present, it SHOULD send a PathErr with the error code "Unknown object class", which makes setup fail. A core node MAY accept EROs that contain only the ingress edge node, ingress core node, egress core node and egress edge node, to support explicit label control. A rejection for any other ERO format SHOULD use the Bad Explicit Route Object error.

If there is no ERO, the core node MUST calculate a route to the destination and put it in an ERO before forwarding, unless the egress edge node is adjacent to that core node. If no route is found, it SHOULD return a PathErr with code and value 24,5, "No route available toward destination". If there is an ERO, the core node SHOULD verify it against its topology database, and returns the same 24,5 error if the route is not viable by topology, resources or local policy.

For explicit label control, the ingress edge node can put egress link and label information in the ERO. If that is the only ERO content, the first subobject is the egress core node's node-ID with the L-bit set, followed by the subobjects that identify the link and labels. If it is the last hop of a longer ERO, the L-bit MAY be clear.
sections.eli5: If the customer does not say which roads to use, the company picks the route itself. If the customer names roads, the company checks they work, and it is allowed to say no.

sections.title: Route Recording and Notification
sections.content:
An edge node MAY include a Record Route Object (RRO). A core node MAY remove it from the Path message before forwarding, and may remove it from a Resv message sent to the edge node, depending on configuration. A core node MAY also edit the RRO in a Resv so that it covers only the subobjects from the egress core node through the egress edge node, which tells the ingress side the link and labels chosen at the far end.

An edge node MAY include a NOTIFY_REQUEST object in the Path and Resv messages it creates, and core nodes may send Notify messages to edge nodes that did. A core node MAY strip the object. If the edge node sent none, the adjacent core node may add one with its own address. In those two cases the core node SHOULD NOT send Notify messages to the edge node. A core node that receives a request MAY replace the Notify node address with its own, and then it MAY forward received Notify messages to the edge node selectively under local policy.
sections.eli5: The company may or may not tell you which roads the truck actually took, and it decides which progress messages are passed on to you.

sections.title: Connection Deletion
sections.content:
Normal RSVP-TE deletion uses a PathTear, or a ResvTear and PathTear together. In optical networks, removing a cross-connect in one node can look like a failure downstream, such as loss of light, and cause management alarms or trigger restoration or protection.

To avoid this, the graceful deletion procedure of RFC 3473 SHOULD be followed: an ADMIN_STATUS object MUST be sent along the path before the connection is actually deleted. If an ingress core node gets a PathTear without having seen that, it MAY pause the tear and first send a Path message with ADMIN_STATUS. After the Resv echoes it, or a timer expires, the node MUST forward the PathTear.

RFC 3473 also adds the Path_State_Removed flag to PathErr. A core node next to an edge node MAY map between ResvTear/PathTear teardown and PathErr with that flag. But a core node that receives a PathErr with Path_State_Removed from downstream MUST NOT retain Path state and send a ResvTear upstream, since that would imply downstream state was retained.
sections.eli5: Before shutting a road, you warn everyone along it, so they do not think there has been an accident and start a rescue.

sections.title: VPN Connections
sections.content:
The extensions are meant to work with VPNs. The core may be a technology other than GMPLS, so no mandatory mapping of core connections to access connections is defined. When the core is GMPLS, the RFC RECOMMENDS a procedure based on LSP hierarchy (RFC 4206).

The VPN connection is modeled as three hops: one for each access link and one across the core. A Path message arriving on a VPN interface is held at the ingress core node while a separate signaling exchange between core nodes, in the core's own address space, sets up the core connection. That connection is then used as a single link in the VPN connection, signaled with an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object. The held Path message is then forwarded in the VPN addressing realm to the core node of the destination edge node. The RFC lists IP and GRE tunnels and BGP/MPLS VPNs as possible ways to do that, and leaves the choice open.
sections.eli5: For a private service, the company first builds one big shared road in the middle, then treats it as one hop between the customer's two ends.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single sentence. The trust model between core and edge differs from the one in RFC 3473, because the core is permitted to hide its topology from edge nodes, and is permitted to restrict what edge nodes can do by filtering out specific RSVP objects. That matches the optional removal of ERO, RRO and Notify objects described elsewhere in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The company does not fully trust customers, so it can hide its maps and throw out requests it does not like.
